one_liner: C++23 consteval FKS perfect-hash unordered_map for compile-time keysets; 1.4-2.9x faster than std::unordered_map in three paper demos.
what_it_does: static_maps is a header-only C++23 library from an arXiv paper. It builds a perfect-hash map entirely at compile time (consteval) when every key is known in advance, such as element symbols, codons or ticker symbols. You write `static constexpr auto m = static_maps::make_unordered_map<data_array>();` (or construct `static_maps::unordered_map(array_of_pairs)` through CTAD) and look up with `m[key]` or `m.at(key)`; a lookup with a constant key folds to a literal. Keys are fixed, but values can change at run time if the map is declared `constinit` instead of `constexpr`; there is no insert, erase, find, count or contains, and the deposit also ships a sorted-array `static_maps::map` and two leaner variants (`unordered_map_small_values`, `DangerousUnorderedMap`).
how_it_is_fast: It uses Fredman-Komlos-Szemeredi (FKS) two-level perfect hashing with multipliers found by a consteval xorshift64* search. The raw hash (DJB2 for string_view, identity for integers) is multiplied by k modulo the largest prime of a 16/32/64-bit SIZE_T and masked into a power-of-two primary table with 8-16 slots per key. A bucket with one key returns at once; a colliding bucket uses its own multiplier and a quadratic-size secondary table. Because the table is collision-free and sits in .rodata, `operator[]` does no key comparison, probing, heap access or run-time construction, and the factory picks the smallest SIZE_T that keeps truncated hashes distinct (adding an XOR salt if needed), with a compare-and-subtract modulo replacing `%` for 64-bit SIZE_T.
when_to_use: Fixed string-to-value tables compiled into the binary (symbol, opcode, keyword, codon or ticker lookups) where every key is known at build time and std::unordered_map is only used as a read-mostly dictionary.
Hot loops where run-time lookups dominate: the codon demo (64 keys, 65,536 lookups per run) showed the largest gain, about 2.9x over std::unordered_map and 2.2x over Frozen (derived from paper data).
Programs that start often or must not allocate at startup: the compiler builds the table and places it in .rodata, so there is no construction cost or heap allocation at run time.

Fixed key universe with changing values, where jitter matters: the 4,042-ticker update demo uses a constinit map with mutable values, and its run-time standard deviation was ±950.6 µs vs ±1660.8 µs for std::unordered_map.
Code that already uses std::string_view keys, builds with a C++23 GCC 15 or Clang 21, and can accept much longer compile times for the tables involved.
when_not_to_use: Keys that are not known until run time, or keysets that change often: there is no insert or erase, and each keyset change is a recompile.
Large keysets or tight build budgets: at 4,042 keys the build took 55.2 s vs 1.5 s for std::unordered_map, raised constexpr limits are required, and nothing larger than 4,042 keys was tested.

Miss-heavy lookups or membership tests: there is no find, contains or count, operator[] returns an arbitrary value or throws for an absent key, and at() reports every miss by throwing std::out_of_range (after an internal throw and catch), which is slow when misses are common.

Cache-constrained large tables: with the default DELTA_PRIMARY=8 each key gets 8-16 primary rows, each holding three SIZE_T fields in three separate arrays, so a lookup can touch several arrays plus the value array; the paper itself warns that a large delta stresses the CPU cache.

Pre-C++23 toolchains, MSVC, -fno-exceptions builds, or teams that need a maintained project: other compilers are not documented, the lookup path uses throw/try/catch, and the code is a one-off figshare deposit whose only test suite belongs to the vendored Frozen.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only; the vendored Frozen 1.1.1 copy is used only by the comparison demos)
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (uses deducing this, std::views::zip/adjacent and constexpr std::vector). Tested only with GCC 15.2.1 and Clang 21.1.6; the paper says earlier working versions are unknown. GCC needs a raised -fconstexpr-ops-limit (and -fconstexpr-loop-limit for large keysets), Clang a raised -fconstexpr-steps, and the 4,042-key demo on Clang also needed -fexperimental-new-constant-interpreter.
integration.platforms: any target with a C++23 GCC or Clang (benchmarked only on x86-64 Linux); the optional USING_UINT128 path needs __uint128_t; MSVC not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; constexpr maps are immutable .rodata data, so concurrent reads share no mutable state, but constinit maps with mutable values have no synchronization
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — you change std:: to static_maps:: and build from a constexpr array of pairs, but only operator[], at(), iteration, size(), keys() and values() exist: no find/count/contains/insert/erase, no custom KeyEqual or Allocator, and operator[] never inserts and can return another key's value for an absent key

gotchas: operator[] does not check the key: an absent key either throws std::out_of_range (empty primary slot) or silently returns another key's value. Use at(), which compares the stored key, whenever input can fall outside the keyset. All published timings use the unchecked operator[].

Builds are not reproducible by default: the RNG seed comes from __DATE__ and __TIME__, so each compile can pick different multipliers, table layout and compile time. The class constructors accept a seed_val argument, but the make_unordered_map factory does not expose one.

Prefer make_unordered_map<data_array>() over the CTAD constructor: the constructor defaults to a 16-bit SIZE_T for up to 255 keys and does not check that truncated raw hashes are distinct. If two keys collide there, the secondary-multiplier search loops until the compiler's constexpr limit aborts the build.

Only constexpr_hashes::hash<std::string_view> (DJB2), <int> and <std::size_t> (identity) exist, and the factory always uses hash<K>, so other key types need your own constexpr specialization. The header also does `using namespace constexpr_hashes;` at file scope and puts helpers such as seed() and RaggedArray in the global namespace, so its `hash` can clash with `using namespace std;`.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick static_maps over frozen when your keys are std::string_view (Frozen needs its own frozen::string type) and lookups dominate: in the paper's demos it beat the vendored Frozen 1.1.1 by 1.25x, 2.25x and 1.03x (derived from paper data), at up to 2.6x Frozen's compile time (55.2 s vs 21.1 s on 4,042 keys). Choose frozen (C++14, also has sets), mph (qlibs) or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash when you need a maintained GitHub project or an older compiler; only Frozen has been benchmarked head-to-head against static_maps.
verified_claims_summary: Per-run time (std::unordered_map built at run time plus lookups, vs static_maps built by the compiler) was 35.8 vs 89.6 µs for 1,024 lookups in an 84-key element table, 607.6 vs 1746.8 µs for 65,536 lookups in a 64-codon table, and 15,295 vs 21,228 µs for about 259k in-place updates in a 4,042-ticker table that the paper calls S&P 500 (2.5x, 2.9x and 1.4x, derived from paper data). The authors measured this in their arXiv preprint with g++ 15.2.1 (libstdc++ inferred), -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native, on an Intel Core i5-1240P laptop at real-time priority with ASLR off; no independent run exists.
status_note: Marked active, but the code is one figshare v1 deposit (2026-02-26) with no repo, issue tracker or later version; it is MIT-licensed and about a dozen small flat headers, so vendoring is the only integration path.
